en: [Pravargya] K1 checked up to 13.10 (108b9) = End of N1.

13.1.1.1. For one who has performed the *pravargya* rite, there are the ritual materials: a wooden sword (*samic*), a spade (*abhri*), a yoke-thong (*yoktra*), and a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). These four are placed to the north of the *āhavanīya* fire.

13.1.1.2. Clay from a pit of compassion (*karuṇīyā mṛd*), earth trampled by a boar, earth from an anthill, saline soil (*utīkāḥ*), and goat’s milk—these five are to be applied in succession at the time of preparing the high altar (*uttaravedi*).

13.1.1.3. Clay from a pit of compassion, goat’s milk as the highest [ingredient], the hair of a black antelope skin, pebbles with goat’s milk, shards of pottery, and the decoction of *parṇa* leaves—these five are to be placed within the shed enclosed by a wall (*pariśrita*) on ground strewn with sand.
13.1.1.4. An inquiry concerning the preparation: Should one prepare the materials for one who is initiated (*dīkṣita*), or for one who is not initiated?

13.1.1.5. If he should prepare them for one who is not initiated, he should melt the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purify it, wipe the *sruva* and *sruk* spoons, go forward to the eastern half of the *āhavanīya* fire, and 13.1.1.6. take four portions of the butter.

13.1.1.7. He offers that [oblation] with the verse, “They harness the mind and they harness the thoughts,” taking a fuel-stick of *vikaṅkata* wood and offering it in the Āhavanīya fire with the words, “The wise ones [offer] the praise of the wise one, svāhā!

13.1.1.8. [The rule is: “One should collect [the fuel-sticks] for the consecrated person while he is performing austerities. Regarding this: 13.1.1.9. With the verse, “They harness the mind and they harness the thoughts,” he places a fuel-stick of *vikaṅkata* wood [on the fire], but he does not offer [an oblation].

13.1.1.10. Others say that he should recite only the *yajus* formula. 13.1.1.11–12. With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ... he takes up the wooden spade made of *vaikaṅkata* wood; with the words, "I take thee at the impulse of the Aśvins; thou art a spade, thou art a woman, a performer of the sacrifice for the gods," [he takes it].
13.1.1.13. With the verse, "Arise, O Brahmanaspati," he stands up, taking hold of both the girdle and the black antelope skin, [reciting]: "Those seeking the gods are with thee. 13.1.1.14.

With the verse, "May Brahmanaspati go forward," he approaches the materials at the site of the high altar (uttaravedi), [reciting]: "May the divine Sūnṛtā come forward; may they worship us. 13.1.1.15.
To the north of the materials, he spreads out the black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and its hairy side upward.
13.1.1.E. "The two goddesses, Heaven and Earth.

Having struck from the clay of the Karuṇīyā [pit] with a clod of earth from a rain-cloud, saying, "O two goddesses, Heaven and Earth, have you approved for me," he carries away half of the black antelope skin, reciting three times: "May I succeed today at the head of Makha; for Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"
13.1.2.2. [He takes] from the earth dug up by a boar with the mantra, "So much was the earth in the beginning"; three times with "May I prosper today..."; 13.1.2.3.
[He takes] from the mound of an anthill with "O divine ants"; three times with "The first-born of this being, according to the Ṛta...";
13.1.2.4. [He takes] from the *ūtikā* plants with "Thou art the vigor of Indra"; three times with "May I prosper today...".

13.1.2.5. With the words, “Thou art born of fire, O Prajāpati, the seed,” he divides the goat’s milk three times. With the words, “May I prosper today, [O] head,” [he takes it]. 13.1.2.6. Having poured all the goat’s milk into clay from a water-pot, having gathered together the edges of the black antelope skin, and having bound it with a yoke-thong, he rises up taking the ritual materials with the words, “Arise, O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati),” and with the words, “[O ye who] desire the gods, [come] together.”

13.1.2.7. With the verse, "May Brahmanaspati come," he approaches the ritual materials mixed with the decoction of *parṇa* leaves, [reciting]: "May the divine Sūnṛtā come toward the heroes; may the gods bring the sacrifice to us, bestowing fivefold wealth.

13.1.2.8. "Many carry [it]," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 13.1.2.9. Having brought it into this enclosed space, he mixes it with the ritual materials containing the *parṇa* decoction, [reciting]: "May Madhu make thee sweet."
13.1.2.10. Having measured out the clay with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," he forms it into a lump.

With the words, "You two are the feet of the sacrifice," he supports [the vessel] with his two thumbs. Having likewise formed three lumps, he gives the first lump to him who makes the *mahāvīra* with the words, "Thou art Gāyatra."

With the formula, "Thou art Traiṣṭubha," he makes the second; with "Thou art Jāgata," the third. With the formula, "I fashion thee with the Gāyatrī metre," he fashions it; with "I fashion thee with the Traiṣṭubha metre" and "I fashion thee with the Jāgata metre," he makes that Mahāvīra pot one span in height, well-proportioned, with three elevations, and with a neck encircled by a girdle.
At the appropriate time, he winds the girdle around it with the formula, "Thou art the girth of Makha."
With the words, “May Aditi grasp your opening,” he makes the opening upward from there.

With the words, “By means of the *pāṅkta* metre,” he makes the drinking-hole with either a bamboo shaft or his thumb. With the words, “Be heated by the heat of Śūrya,” and with the words, “You are Makha; for Makha, you!”—having thus prepared the *mahāvīra*, he sets it down. He prepares the other *mahāvīra* silently. He prepares the two *avāñjana* stones. He prepares the two *rauhiṇa* potsherds. He prepares the butter-pot; it may be one made by a potter.

They cause [the trees] to be planted; they wash them with cleansing waters; they [anoint them] with *klītaka* and smooth bamboo stalks and stones. When he thinks they have been planted, then, intending to fumigate them, he gathers the ritual materials.

Then, intending to fumigate... (9) they pile up horse-dung, cow-dung, large clods of earth, dried grass, and wood, as well as the milk of a cow and a goat, to the north of the hall; they dig a square pit there. Having enclosed that area and brought fire from another source, he lights three pieces of horse-dung and throws them one by one into the *mahāvīra* vessel with the formula, “Thou art the footprint of the bull, the horse; O Varuṇa, [I place thee] according to the law. He throws the others silently.

With the formula, "Aditi, thee," he digs with a wooden shovel into the pit already dug, [saying]: "May the divine one, favored by all the gods, dig the hole in the dwelling-place of the earth, like Aṅgiras. Having strewn the pit with heating-stones (śrapaṇas) and having encircled the Mahāvīra vessel with two enclosing-sticks, he places it down with the formula, "For radiance thee—for heat thee."

Having silently placed the other [sacrificial items] and covered them with the cooking vessels, he stands over them with kindling sticks, [reciting]: "O most glorious one, [shine] forth toward heaven with greatness. He should neither breathe upon them nor cast a shadow over them. With this very verse, "Toward this [fire] with greatness toward heaven," he gazes at the ritual procedure with friendliness.
When he considers them to be well-smoked, he then takes up the fire-shovel made of *vikaṅkata* wood, [reciting]: "For success, thee!"

With the words, "May Savitṛ the god lift thee up," he throws out the embers with the wooden shovel. With the words, "O thou of fair hands, fair fingers, and fair arms, and capable," while not letting it fall to the earth, he causes it to be raised. With the words, "Fill the regions and the quarters," and "Arise, become great; stand upright, thou art firm," having grasped the Mahāvīra vessel with the two supporting rings, and having shaken off the smoke, he gazes at it with the formula, "For the sake of the Sun's splendor—for thy prosperity."

With the words, "For security, thee," he places [the first jar] in the pit of the well; having silently lifted the others, he places them in the very same pit of the well. Then he surrounds this one with embers, saying: "Here I enclose myself and so-and-so, the son of such-a-man, with splendor and sacred knowledge... here I enclose myself and so-and-so, the son of such-a-man, with offspring and cattle; here I enclose myself and so-and-so, the son of such-a-man, with the kingdom and poison. He surrounds the others silently.

Then he pushes out the embers from this [spot] toward the west, saying: "Here I exclude so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, from the kingdom, from the people, from the subjects, from cattle, from splendor, and from Vedic luster.

He pushes them out silently for the others. Having taken the *mahāvīra* vessel with his two hands and placed it in a pan or a shallow bowl, he sprinkles it with goat's milk, saying: "With the *gāyatra* [verse], I sprinkle thee as an oblation.
He causes it to overflow with cow's milk silently.
The other [vessels] he silently rinses with goat's milk and causes them to overflow with cow's milk;
having made them cool and placed them together in the *upayamanī* tray, he gathers the ends of the black antelope skin, ties them with the yoke-halter, takes them up, and stands nearby.
Having entered the hall by the eastern door, he places the *anvita* vessel near the women to the north-east of the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "O divine leader, sit down; I seat thee.
(Śrautasūtra 13.4)

Intending to proceed with the *pravargya* rite, he gathers the materials: two *mahāvīra* vessels, two *avāṣṭhya* vessels, two *rauhiṇa* potsherds, two *parigharmya* vessels, one silver and one gold [vessel], two *ākharau* pits, a vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), a dipping-spoon (*pratipū*), and sand; these are the twelve earthen items. There are two mats made of *muñja* grass, cuttings of *muñja* grass, a cord made of *muñja* grass, and two loops for binding made of *muñja* grass.

These are the six medicinal herbs; five *dhṛṣṭi* and *dhāvitra* fans; three *śaphopayāma* vessels; two *parigharmya* pegs; two *rohiṇa-havana* ladles; a *vaikaṅkata* *pracaraṇī* large ladle and a *vaikaṅkata* *sruva* small dipping-spoon; thirteen *vaikaṅkata* enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) for use; twelve *paryavacayana* sticks with fuel-sticks as the seventh; three enclosing-sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood; a central post (*methī*) made of *udumbara* wood; and a peg for the she-goat.

Having set down these wooden sacrificial implements and having carried forward the waters, he offers the *prāyaṇīya* oblation; having performed the *prāyaṇīya*, he purchases the King (Soma); having purchased the King, he causes [the cow] to be milked and offers the *ātithya* to him; having performed the *ātithya*, he issues the command: "O *Āgnīdh*, place the two *rauhiṇa* cakes on the fire; O *Pratiprasthātṛ*, set down the *pravargya* equipment. They do this:

the *Āgnīdh* places the two *rauhiṇa* cakes on the fire, the *Pratiprasthātṛ* sets down the *pravargya* equipment, and to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire he pours out sand; he spreads that out into a pit.

To the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he scatters sand; he spreads that out exactly like a pit (ākhará). To the north-east of the Āhavanīya, he scatters sand along the track of the *pratiprasthātṛ*; he spreads that out exactly like a pit. Having brought the Mahāvīra pot with the supporting ladle (*upayamanī*), he places it to the north of the upper pit. Having encircled the Mahāvīra with the two enclosing-sticks (*parigrahaṇī*), he places it behind the pit. He covers it with a Veda-broom made of Muñja grass. With a *pracaraṇī* ladle made of Vikaṅkata wood, he prepares the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*) provided with strainers (*pavitra*).
There, he places another mound to the west; upon it, he spreads a grass mat made of muñja grass;
the Āgnīdhra sets down the two Rauhiṇa cakes, which have been spread with a base of ghee and sprinkled over; he places them in front of the mound, facing westward.

Without crossing over, he makes the right one the uppermost; they bring [the materials]: the cords for binding and yoking. They place those to the east of the pit (akhara); they bring the two *avārṣṭhya* stones; they place those to the east of the pit itself. They bring five stirring-sticks (*dhṛṣṭi*), three winnowing-sieves (*śapoyāma*), three enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood, a central post (*methī*) made of *udumbara* wood, a peg for the she-goat, and bundles of *muñja* grass.

[The priests] thus bring forward all the ritual implements; when this has been arranged, the officiating priests enter, they close the doors, and [the priest recites]: "The friend impels the people; may he, knowing, be a friend to the mortal, full of refreshment. Having approached, they stand nearby; with the words, "Through these songs may we be masters," they sit down separately.

To the south, the *brahmán* and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) sit down; behind them, the *hotṛ* sits turned toward the east, and the *pratiprasthātṛ* sits turned toward the north. Then he looks at the officiating priests, saying: "The *gharma*-vessels are bellies..."

Having grasped the *mahāvīra* with the two formulas for grasping, "The heats, the bellies, the suns, the dwellings, the two seers, Mātariśvan—make me glorious among this people, a beautiful eater of food," he wipes it with a cord of *muñja* grass. With the formula, "Thou art the conqueror, the overcomer of rivals; they set thee down boldly as the overcomer of rivals," he wipes the pit (*ākhara*). He wipes everything that has fallen off. Having become the *pratiprasthātṛ*, he first wipes the pit. [He places] the silver vessel for the *parigharma*.

Having taken [the vessel], he draws a line around the middle of the northern pit; he hides that silver [vessel] for the boiling milk, saying: "Be united with the earth! Protect [us] from the earth! You are the interior of the earth; protect us from the heat of the earth!"—thus, having enclosed the *mahāvīra* with the two enclosures, at the morning performance he places it in the middle of the western pit, and at the evening performance he places it behind;
he worships the settled [vessel] with: "Sit happily! You are great! and with: "Shine forth—you who are beautiful to behold!"

Then, when they restore the head of the sacrifice, [he recites]: "With the mouths of the Vedas, I praise Agni, the domestic priest; for food thee, for strength thee; O Agni, come for the feast; with the hands of the god Savitṛ, I restore the head of the sacrifice.
Then he wipes [the fire] toward his face from the sprinkling waters, saying: "With the hands of the god Savitṛ, I anoint thee with divine ointment."

Having touched the *madantī* waters and taken up the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters, while rising, he issues the call: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Hotṛ, recite for the *gharma*; O Prastotṛ, chant the *sāman*!"—thus [he addresses] Vācaspati.

(5) You are the portion of the bull; for them, I turn you toward them. Sing forth to this Indu, O men, for Pavamāna; he indeed desires to sacrifice to the gods. Sing most exalted praise to this god Agni; may he come with the gods to our seat; may he, the best of sacrificers, sit upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). We bring you hither like a chariot for protection and for favor—Indra, the crusher of enemies. O Indra, most powerful Lord of the True, that nourishment of the god Savitṛ we choose; may it be the most excellent, bestowing all things.

The Adhvaryu mutters the introductory verse of the *uktha*, "We meditate upon the son of Raṃbhaga"; he mutters the impulse (*prasava*), "And he who, having gone forth..."; the Brahman [recites]: "May the *stobhas* carry Viṣṇu, who is approved by all the gods and the Maruts, whose sky is anointed with *sāmans* and who is well-disposed; shining, bestow upon us a state free from anger! Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ om! Accompanied by Indra, proceed! With the words, "For Agni thee," he sprinkles the *mahāvīra* vessel; [with the words], "For Vāyu thee."
"‘For Vāyu thee, for Yama thee, for Makha thee, for Subhūta thee, for Brahman-splendor thee— I sprinkle thee,’ with these words he sprinkles the excavation;
he sprinkles everything that has fallen away."
Having first run to the front pit, the Pratiprasthātṛ sprinkles the front pit;
having poured into the pit whatever remains of the *prokṣaṇī* water, and having set down the *pracaraṇī* ladle, he turns toward the southern shoulder.

The Pratiprasthātṛ and the Agnīdh receive these sprinkled [pieces of wood], seven pieces of wood including one fuel-stick (*samit*). The Pratiprasthātṛ receives thirty enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood; having run to the two fires, the Pratiprasthātṛ lays down the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood with the formula: "O Gandharvas, finders of wealth! For all your thoughts I entrust you; be yoked for the service of the gods. Along the joints of those [enclosing sticks], the Agnīdh places the two [fire-wood] bundles made of *dru* wood without crossing them over, making the southern one the uppermost.
The Pratiprasthātṛ places seven pieces of wood, including one for the fuel, to the north of the Āhavanīya fire.

Taking that sprinkled Udumbara post—which serves as the tethering peg for the she-goat—he carries it out by the front of the Gārhapatya and behind the Anvāhāryapacana, and having brought it out through the southern door, they fix the sacrificial grass (barhis) to the south of the post. He places the post behind the she-goat's tethering peg;
when he perceives [the priest reciting], "I have praised the god Savitṛ," [he proceeds].
Then he anoints the Mahāvīra with clarified butter, saying, "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey.
Having grasped the Mahāvīra with a cord made of Muñja grass, he places it in his left hand, saying, "O leader of the gods, may you come to me.

While holding the Mahāvīra, he draws out embers from the north and, having blown upon them, offers ten breath-oblations (prāṇāhuti), saying: "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Vyāna, svāhā! To Apāna, svāhā! To the eye, svāhā! To the ear, svāhā! To the mind, svāhā! To Speech, Sarasvatī, svāhā! To Dakṣa, svāhā! To Kṛ... [the rest of the verse]."

With the formula, "Thou art flame," the Pratiprasthātṛ kindles the bundles of muñja grass; with "Thou art radiance, thou art light, thou art heat," and "Thou art splendor," he places them within the pit with their tips pointing in various directions;
with "Thou art bright," they anoint the Mahāvīra vessel upon them.
With the verse, "Whom the sages proclaim," he fills the Mahāvīra with clarified butter.

With the verse, "Like one possessing omenta, he has eaten the food by means of Agni," and with "Invincible in front," he measures it on all sides with his span without touching it. With "In the overlordship of Agni, give me life and fatness," [he measures] in front; with "Possessing sons from the south," in the south; with "In the overlordship of Indra, give me offspring," with the *śuṣadā* [formula], in the west; and with "In the overlordship of the god Savitṛ, give me breath," in the north.
"To the north, the Āśruti," he says as he places [the stone] to the north, with the words: "Under the overlordship of Mitra and Varuṇa, grant me hearing.
"Above, the Vidhṛti," he says as he places [the stone] above, with the words:

"Under the overlordship of Bṛhaspati, grant me spiritual power (brahman), grant me ruling power (kṣatra), bestow splendor upon me, bestow luster upon me, bestow glory upon me, bestow nourishment upon me, bestow mind upon me."
With the words, "Thou art the comforter of men," he touches her, saying, "May she have many sons for me; do not harm me.
With the words, "Thou art bold; bestow the sacred word (brahman)," he takes up the fire-stirring stick made of *vaikaṅkata* wood.
"Thou art bold; bestow sovereignty," with these words he hands it to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
With "O Agni, burn up the enemies within," he pushes away the embers from the Mahāvīra. With "Burn the curse of the hostile stranger;

O unwearying one," and "Ye are piled, ye are piled around," he covers the Mahāvīra with embers by means of a shovel, saying: "Svāhā! Be surrounded by the Maruts; O lover of songs, may the songs be a source of delight for thee."

With the formula, "Thou art a measure," he encloses it with enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *vaikaṅkata* wood— some with their tips pointing eastward and others with their tips pointing northward—

silently inserting them in between while the Pratiprasthātṛ arranges them around. With the formulas, "Thou art a measure, thou art a counter-measure, thou art a measuring-out, thou art a measuring-together,

thou art a measuring-up," and "Thou art the concealment of the intermediate space," he removes the thirteenth stick from the south, placing it facing eastward with the formula, "Protect the intermediate space from the heat."

With the mantra, “Protect from contact with heaven,” he places a golden disk (*rukma*) on top. With the mantra, “Thou art the interior of heaven; protect me from the heat of heaven,” he [places it] in front during the morning performance and behind during the evening performance. He worships with the mantra, “Worthy, thou bearest...”; [he addresses] the arrows, the bows, the *aṣka*, and the great worshipful one: “Worthy, thou leadest all this world; O Rudra, there is nothing stronger than thee; let another be superior to thy brilliance.”
With the words, "Thou art gāyatra," he takes up the shortest fan;

with "Thou art traiṣṭubha," the longer one; and with "Thou art jāgata," having become like a weaver, he fans [the fire] upward with all the blades together, using their hair-side, saying, "Honey! Honey! Honey!"
Having risen, he hands the larger of those two to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
Of those two, the elder one, they pass around three times from left to right while fanning; when they have passed around three times, the Adhvaryu takes up the *dhavitra*.

He hands himself over to the east and the fire to the west to the Pratiprasthātṛ. Of those two, the one who is older sits down facing away from the Āgnīdhra. The Adhvaryu sits behind him, turned toward the east; the Pratiprasthātṛ from the north, turned toward the south; and the Āgnīdhra from the front, turned toward the west.
Accomplishing their task, they shake [the fires] at the ends of the *praṇava* syllables, without letting them roll forward.
When it blazes, then, having taken the gold to be heated, he hides it in the *mauñja* grass-bundle on the *veda*.
When he knows [the verse], "O Aśvins, may our speech be effective," then they lift up the fans.
When he knows [the verse], "The dappled one has shone at the head of the dawns," then they rise, saying, "The *gharma* has shone."

At the morning performance, the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite: "Shine forth tenfold in the east," and "Tenfold in the south, tenfold in the west, tenfold in the north—may the Gharma shine. And:
"May Agni with the Vasus [place] thee in the east... may radiance [be] in me."
During the evening circuit, shaking [the fans] three times, they go around each path;
having set aside their fans and stood according to the available space, they worship with the verse: "I saw the herdsman...

I have seen the herdsman who never stumbles; he has shone together with Savitṛ, together with Sūrya. As the upholder of heaven, you shine through the mid-air and the earth; you are the upholder of the wide firmament, the upholder, the god among gods, the immortal one born of fervor. For the heart, thee; for the mind, thee. Extend the protection of the *yoga* for all beings, O lord of the minds of all, lord of the speech of all, lord of the glory of all, lord of the fervor of all, lord of the light of all!

"O Lord of Prayer (*brahmaṇaspati*), you who hear the gods, O divine one, bringer of the law of the gods, let the enemies be right here; may Heaven and Earth yield to you both! Homage to Heaven! Homage to Earth!"—with the words "May I consort with thee through Tvaṣṭṛ," he causes the wives to be led away behind the cloth by means of the *veda*-grass-bundle. Having approached with the formula "O thou of heroic seed, may I be united with thee for the increase of wealth," and having run back, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the southern *rauhiṇa* cake with the formula: "May the Day, the light, be pleased with its banner; the fair-lighted one, with the lights, Svāhā!"

At the morning performance, [he offers with] “The night has shone forth with its light and banner, svāhā! At the evening performance, when he knows [the verse], “I invoke this well-milking cow,” then, at the binding of the tethering-rope, both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer take hold [of it] with: “By the hands of the god, I take thee; thou art the girdle of Aditi.”
With the words, “Thou art the turban of Aditi,” the Pratiprasthātṛ and the Agnīdh both seize the halter. The Agnīdh runs out in front of the Gārhapatya fire, and the Pratiprasthātṛ behind it.
He calls out loudly, “So-and-so, come here! using whatever the cow’s name may be;
he calls out in a low voice, “Iḍā, come here! and then again loudly, “So-and-so, come here! using whatever the cow’s name may be.
With "Come, Aditi! he calls out in a low voice; with "So-and-so, come! he calls out aloud according to the cow's name;
with "O Sarasvatī, come! he calls out in a low voice; with "Vāyu is yours; may Pūṣan release you," he releases the calf; and with "Let the Aśvins cause it to be given."
He recites, "That breast of thine," and says, "The refreshing, bliss-giving one has been made for suckling.

He touches the calf with the words, "O cow, protect the *gharma* on your head; O cow, drink the *gharma* on your head. He binds it with the words, "For the *gharma*, O head! and "I bind thee for the Aśvins."

"Bṛhaspati shall sit down beside you," with these words he sits down; "O ye givers, O ye full ones," with these words he touches the udders; "Enveloped on all sides by the red," and "Swell for the Aśvins," with these words he causes the lower lip to swell; "Swell for Sarasvatī, swell for Pūṣan, swell for Bṛhaspati, swell for Indra, swell for Indra."
They milk the cow silently into the vessel; they suckle the goat silently at the udder.

When he knows [the verse], "Arise, O Brahmanaspati," then he rises. When he knows [the verse], "He has milked the swelling abundance," then the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer, having taken up the tethering-strap and the fastening-rope, enter [the shed].
The Pratiprasthātṛ alone holds the milks and pushes back the embers from the Mahāvīra;

having ensured they are well-pushed-back, he touches the southern foot with the formula, "Thou art Gāyatra," the northern one with "Thou art Traiṣṭubha," and the supporting base with "Thou art Jāgata."
When he knows, "The distress is gone," then they cause the milk-cows to be led forward.
The Āgnīdhra runs out in front of the Gārhapatya fire, while the Pratiprasthātṛ follows behind;
[the Adhvaryu] awaits him as he brings [the milk], saying, "Come hither with a portion of strength," and "O Indra and Aśvins, [with] the honey of the bees."
"Bring it," he said;
the Āgnīdhra brings the goat's milk.
"Bring it! he says; the Āgnīdhra brings it. Having reached it, [the Adhvaryu] says: "O Vasus, drink the *gharma*, sacrifice, *vaṣaṭ*!
*Svāhā*, I offer you to the rain-seeking ray of the sun—*vaṣaṭ*. He gazes at the rising smoke, saying: "You are the honey-oblation; heat the heat of the sun!
"Bring it! he says; he brings it.
The Pratiprasthātṛ silently pours the milk from the *upayamanī* into that very vessel.
He encloses the *mahāvīra* with two enclosures, saying, "I enclose thee for Heaven and Earth.
He supports it with the *upayamanī*, saying, "I support thee with the intermediate space. [He says,] "May I be able to bear thee, permitted by the gods and the ancestors."
When he perceives, "Arise, O Brahmanaspati," then they arise;
when he perceives, "Upward, O God Savitṛ, with golden hands," then they lift up the pole;
when he perceives, "Let Brahmanaspati go forward," then they step forward toward the east.

"Thou art brilliance; follow after brilliance! Thou art light; follow after light! Thou art heaven; follow after heaven! Touching the sky, do not harm me; touching the intermediate space, do not harm me; touching the earth, do not harm me! Thou art heaven; grant me heaven; granting me heaven, protect me from heaven!"—thus [he says]. With the formula, "To the ocean, to thee, to Vāta, svāhā!", the Adhvaryu mutters the seven names of Vāta without taking breath: "To Śalila, to thee, to Vāta... to Vāta, svāhā"—thus he mutters through the seven [names], without taking breath.

"To Agni, accompanied by the Vasus, svāhā! To Soma, accompanied by Rudra, svāhā! To Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, svāhā! To Varuṇa, accompanied by the Ādityas, svāhā! To Bṛhaspati, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, svāhā! To Yama, accompanied by Aṅgiras and the Pitṛs, svāhā!"—thus he breathes out upon these seven alone.

With the words, “*divi dhā*,” the Brahman priest causes the sacrificer to recite: “Place this sacrifice, this very sacrifice, in heaven! Go to heaven; go to the fathers who drink the *gharma*. Having performed the sacrifice, may the *stobhas*—approved by all the gods, by the Maruts, and by the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇās*), extended and leading to the further shore—carry you, O singers, with well-disposed minds, along with the *sāmans*, to the gods who drink the *gharma*. *Svāhā* to Agni, the worthy of sacrifice! May there be peace through the *yajus* formulas in all directions.”
Having said, "The Dakṣiṇasād has sacrificed here to all the gods; Svāhā! Drink of the clarified butter, the hot milk, and the honey, O Aśvins," the Brahman sits down.

The Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite, "O Aśvins, drink the hot milk! May Heaven and Earth favor you with their daily aids; homage to Heaven, homage to Earth! Then the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Bring it! and brings it forward.
Having stepped across to the *upayamanī* ladle and the *mahāvīra* vessel, he causes the announcement to be made, saying, "O, announce! He says, "Recite the offering prayer for the *gharma*.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering with: "Svāhā to the Aśvins! Svāhā to Sarasvatī! Svāhā to Pūṣan! Svāhā to Bṛhaspati! Svāhā to Indra! Svāhā to Indra Vaṭ!
When the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.
"O Aśvins, you have drunk the hot milk"—with these words the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite. "'The heart-encompassing from the earth'—'bring it!
thus he says, and the Pratiprasthātṛ brings it indeed with the *upayamanī* ladle into the *mahāvīra*.
When it overflows, then he makes him recite: "Swell for the sake of nourishment (*iṣ*).”
"Make me swell for food, make me swell for strength—for preeminence, make me swell!"—with these words he shakes it, saying: "For splendor thee! For power thee! For prosperity thee!"

"Dharmāsi sudharmā"—with these words, another steps across the altar. "O Agni, maintain our sacred formulations (*brahmāṇi*), maintain our powers (*kṣatrāṇi*), maintain the people (*viśaḥ*); let not the wind cause thee to fall. If he should practice sorcery, he places the *mahāvīra* vessel on the mound, saying: "I place thee in the breath of so-and-so; go forth to ruin along with so-and-so—him who hates us and whom we hate.
Having touched the boiling water (*madantīḥ*), he takes up six fragments (*chākalān*).

Having anointed each one of them individually with clarified butter, he throws them into the Āhavanīya fire while offering oblations: having first offered with "To Pūṣan, the arrow, svāhā!", he places it within the altar;
having offered the second with "To the pressing-stones, svāhā!", he places it in that very same place.
Having offered the third oblation with “To the Pratirebhas, svāhā!”, he places it right here.

Having offered the fourth oblation with “To Heaven and Earth, svāhā!”, he hides it within the enclosing sticks. Having offered the fifth oblation with “To the Fathers who drink the Gharma, svāhā!”, he places it to the south, outside the altar.

Having anointed and offered the sixth portion with the formula, “To Rudra, for thee, for Rudra-hotṛ, svāhā!,” he throws it out to the north outside the *bahirvedi* area while not looking at it. Having touched the *madantī* waters, having grasped the *mahāvīra* vessel with the two grasping formulas, and having poured the residue into the *upayamanī* ladle, he places a fuel-stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood upon the *upayamanī* while holding onto it, reciting at the morning performance: “Thou hast carried me across from day to night; protect me; may she not harm me.”

With the mantra, “May you carry me across from night and from day; protect me, O Agni, from the footless one,” he offers the first oblation with “Bhūḥ svāhā” during the evening performance. Between the two oblations, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the northern *rauhiṇa* cake with the mantra, “Day is light by its banner, the light of lights, svāhā,” during the morning performance.
During the evening performance, he offers this same [cake] with the mantra, “Night is light... svāhā.”
Here he throws the *śakalā* wood chips after [the offering]; he silently offers the second oblation;
having moved [the fire] forward and set down the supporting ladles (*upayamanī*), he wipes [the fire] with the formula, "Fill the cow-pen," and a second time with, "May wealth [fill] my fingers."
With the words, “May the *girasaḥ* eat you, O *havir*,” the Adhvaryu eats from the hand by means of his breath and performs the ritual purification (*mārjana*).

With the words, “May the *girasaḥ* eat you, O *satyahavis*,” he turns back toward the west and takes the portion for consumption (*bhakṣa*) for the Hotṛ, saying, “The oblation is offered; the honey-oblation is for Indra; do not harm me.”
The Hotṛ eats first, then the Adhvaryu, then the Brahman, then the Pratiprasthātṛ, then the Āgnīdhra, and then the sacrificer;
they eat by means of their vital breaths.
The eating of the sacrificer is direct. Having washed the *pratipāvarī* and the *upayamanī* ladles very clean, he places them within the altar after the *ativālī*.

Having brought water for it and placed the golden *parigharma* (milk-vessel) into it, they touch it together with the formula, "May the waters be friendly to us... [we have not cursed our enemies]. Taking the golden *parigharma*, he hides it within the *mauñja* *veda* (grass-broom).
Having poured out the water right there within the altar (*antarvedi*) and having wiped it very clean with the *mauñja* *veda*, he covers the two *mauñja* brooms upon this *veda*.
Having grasped the Mahāvīra with both hands, he places it on the Upayamanī;
he places it on the Avāṣṭhyā; he places it on the Rauhiṇa-offering ladles.
He places all the fragments there; right there the butter-pot and the two Rauhiṇa potsherds lie remaining.
Having fashioned them like gold or like a boat, rising up, he says: "Recite for the Gharma as it is being removed."

Having carried it forward past the Āhavanīya fire, he places it on the throne-seat of the Sovereign (*samrāj*). At the morning performance, he says: "Svāhā! To you, for the rays of the sun"; at the evening performance, he says: "Svāhā! To you, for the constellations. Having sprinkled water, he releases the two traces from the northern side.
He releases the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*);
they attain peace.
Intending to remove the *pravargya* vessel, he gathers the materials: three fire-sticks (*śālākā*), clarified butter, curds, honey, a water-pitcher, and an *avakā* plant.
At the final performance, having offered a drop of curds into the *mahāvīra* vessel and having performed the final *upasad* rite, he places the three fire-sticks to the north of the *āhavanīya* fire.
A Brāhmaṇa sits by the *uttaravedi* with clarified butter, curds, honey, a water-pitcher, and an *avakā* plant.

Having brought the throne-seat (*āsandī*) for the Sovereign King in front of the *āhavanīya* fire, he places it to the north of the *āhavanīya*. Having brought the *mahāvīra* vessel with the supporting ladle (*upayamanī*), he places it upon the throne-seat.
He places the two *avaṣṭhyau* [stones]; he places them at the *rauhiṇa* oblation;
he digs up the *audumbara* sacrificial post-stake, the peg for the goat, and the bundles of *muñja* grass—thus he places everything belonging to the *pariśāṭhalya*.

Having sprinkled water on the two northern pits, he pours grain into a winnowing basket and places it on the *āsandi* (throne-seat). Into the other [basket], having poured sand for the *prativāvarī*, they carry it to the site of the *mārjālīya* fire-altar. Right there, the vessel for the clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) is already placed, as well as the *sruva*-ladle; thus the preparations are completed. Then the *adhvaryu*, having first kindled a *śālāka* (fire-brand) and holding it at the height of the neck, offers an oblation over it with the formula: "Homage to Rudra who dwells in heaven, whose arrows are the rain! Do not strike me together with him; do not harm me, O stealer of heat, O burner in heaven! That which is in the *gāyatrī*—with this I worship thee, svāhā!"
Having offered, he throws it after.

Having kindled a second splinter and holding it at the height of the navel, he makes an oblation, saying: "Obeisance to Rudra who dwells in the intermediate space, whose arrows are the winds; with him may I be united; do not harm me, O Gharma-goer! I sacrifice in the intermediate space—svāhā!
Having thus offered, he throws it after.

Having lit the third splinter and holding it at the height of the knees, he makes an offering, or having cast it [into the fire], [he says]: "Homage to Rudra who dwells on the earth! May I not come into conflict with him whose food is arrows; do not harm me, O Gharma-goer! Whatever heat there is on the earth that belongs to the Jagatī meter—with that I appease thee, svāhā! Having taken the vessel of clarified butter together with the *sruva* ladle, they proceed, standing at the edge of the altar, [reciting]: "May Anumati favor us today; mayest thou, O Anumati, grant us thy consent. Then he says: "Command the *śāman*!"
The Prastotṛ sings the *pravargya-sāman*;

they approach the *nidhana* three times; each person approaches the *nidhana*. They step forward facing east with the words: "For the protection from heaven," "Protect the bodies of the intermediate space," and "By the law of the earth, we follow thee for new prosperity."
Standing by the Audumbarī post, he says, "O Prastotṛ, sing the Śāman!
Thus the Prastotṛ sings the Pravargya-Śāman;
they reach the Nidhana three times, and each person reaches the Nidhana individually.

With the words, "For the protection of the breath from behind thee," they step forward toward the east. With the words, "Protect the bodies of the nobility; we follow thee by the law of the common people for new prosperity," he stands at the time of the *uparava* holes and says, "Sing the *sāman*! The *prastotṛ* sings the *pravargya-sāman* itself;
they reach the finale (*nidhana*) three times, and each individual reaches the finale.

With the words, “For the protection of the breath (prāṇa), thee! they step forward toward the east. Having ascended with the words, “Protect the bodies of the eye; by the law of the ear, we follow after thee for new prosperity,” he places the throne of the sovereign (samrāj) to the north of the northern navel. Having descended, he says, “Sprinkle around! Taking the water-pitcher, the sprinkler goes around three times, sprinkling as he strides forward, with the words, “Thou art pleasant, for the sake of peace; a child, for the sake of supporting people.”
Having set down the pitcher for the sake of sprinkling around again, he scatters [the grass] three times while returning along the path;
having climbed back up, he spreads it out facing away with the mantra, "Drive away hatred, drive away crookedness."
He threshes or winnows, or sweeps away [the chaff], with the verse: "We follow another part of the vow.

With the words, "The navel is four-cornered," he touches the northern navel; and with the words, "The seat of Order, all-encompassing, the wide-extending shelter," having sprinkled [it], he pours the two mounds of earth from the north onto the northern navel.
Having fashioned that four-cornered pit facing east by means of the two *rauhiṇa* oblations, he covers it with *avakā* plants.

Having enclosed the *mahāvīra* vessel with the two enclosures and having placed gold within it, he sets it down in the eastern half of the pit with the formula: "Thou art a fair one, a child for the nourisher of peace; a youth for the nourisher of people.
He silently places the *upaśaya* ladle first in the western enclosure.
At the time for the head, he touches the Mahāvīra vessel while muttering the formula:
"O head, speak and carry forth, and carry around," according to Pariśāṭhala; at the time for the hair, he mutters the *yajus* formula.
Having untied the girdle made of muñja grass, he stretches it eastward so that it touches the *mahāvīra* vessel while saying, "Hair!
Having untied it at the place of the eyes and fastened the two *parigharmya* vessels onto the cords, he interlaces them with the other *mahāvīra* vessel.
He makes the southern one of silver, saying, "The two eyes.
At the time for the tongue, he stretches out a western spade made of *vaikaṅkata* wood so as not to touch the *mahāvīra* pot, saying, "The tongue.
At the time for the beard, having loosened the girdle made of *muñja* grass, he stretches it out toward the west so as not to touch the *mahāvīra* pot, saying, "The beard."
At the time of the collarbones, he touches the two hooves while saying, “The collarbones.
At the time of the shoulders, he stretches out the two backward-turned forefeet while saying, “The shoulders,” so that the two hooves touch them.
At the time of the hands, he stretches out the two backward-turned... [the two] *kaṅkata* hair-combs for the offering, so that the two forefeet touch them.

Saying, “The two hands,” he stretches out the Audumbara *methī* post toward the west at the time of the self. Saying, “The self,” he stretches out the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood toward the east on both sides of the *methī* post, touching it, at the time of the rains. Saying, “The rains,” he stretches out the enclosing-sticks made of *kīkaṭa* wood toward the east, touching the *methī* post, at the time of the *kīkaṭas*. Saying, “The *kīkaṭas*,” he stretches them out, touching the *methī* post.
Over them he spreads fans with the wool facing upwards.

Verily, the vital breaths (prāṇas) impel a man upwards; saying "the vital breaths," he spreads a Vaikaṅkata offering-ladle at the place of the heart, so that it touches the central pillar from the west.

Saying "the heart," he stretches out the western *audumbara* supporting-post (*upayamanī*) so that it touches the central post (*methī*), saying "the two kidneys. Saying "the belly," he stretches out the western *audumbara* supporting-post at the time of the belly so that it touches the central post.

Not making contact with it in the binding of the fastening-ropes, he fixes two [stakes] at the time of the *nikośya*, directed westward, saying, “intestines and bowels” (*āntra-gudā*); [he] stretches them so they are touched...
saying, “[the two] *nikośyas*,” at the time of the *achronya*, he stretches a stake for the goat transversely and upward, so that it touches the stakes, saying, “the hips” (*śroṇī*).
At the time of the *sakthi*, he places two *vaikaṅkata* fire-sticks for the rain, touching them at the points where they meet; saying, "The two thighs," he places a peg between the two thighs.
At the time of the *vasti*, having poured clarified butter into another vessel, he places the butter-pot so that it touches [the peg], saying, "The bladder.
At the time of the *pramehaṇa*, he places a westward-pointing *vaikaṅkata* dipping-spoon so that it touches the pot, saying, "The urethra."
At the time for the marrow, he causes the flour of the *rauhiṇa* cakes to be ground up while saying, "Marrow.

At the time for the skin, he covers it with a black antelope skin, with the neck pointing eastward and the hair facing upward, while saying, "Skin. At the time for the hair, he causes tufts of *muñja* grass to be blown toward the west while saying, "Hair."
With the words, "Thou dost blow forth and thou dost blow around," he mutters the *yajus* of Pariśāṭhala;
having loosened the Udumbara throne-seat, he causes it to fall down toward the north,
and in the middle, with the sound "vād," he performs all the actions as if they were not circular.
Having covered it with a black antelope skin, he pours water into the mahāvīra vessel.
He pours water into the mahāvīra vessel.
He brings all the other [substances] into contact with it,
saying, "Thou art the milk of the earth, ordained among the gods," as he pours the clarified butter;
into that very [butter], he brings all the others into contact, saying, "We pour thee, the vigorous one, for the vigorous ones."
With the words, "Half of the mind is heavenly," he pours curd;
into that very substance, he causes all the others to touch. With the words, "You are the light of the trees, the essence of the plants," he pours honey;
into that very substance, he causes all the others to touch.
He pours water on top;
he causes all the other [substances] to touch [it], and then he prepares the food, saying: "O Gharma, this is your food; may we prepare it for you."

Having made the food possessed of breath, he says: "May I be united with life-span, united with out-breath, united with diffused breath, united with in-breath, united with up-breath, united with middle-breath, united with sight, united with hearing, united with mind, united with speech, and united with skill and resolve. May that one who hates us and whom we hate be separated! Having thus made it possessed of breath, he worships it with the lightning formulas.

"Whichever lightning there was in the east, I have sacrificed; whichever lightning there was in the south, I have sacrificed; whichever lightning there was in the west, I have sacrificed; whichever lightning there was in the north, I have sacrificed; whichever lightning there was above, I have sacrificed. Having thus paid homage with these formulas concerning the lightnings, he descends and says, "Recite the *śamanī*. The *prastotṛ* sings the *vārṣāhara* *sāman* and the *iṣṭāhotrīya*.
When he recognizes [the sound] as "the ocean, the treasure," he then causes rain to fall three times from a water-vessel with the verse: "The sky has leaped down; may we be born upon the earth."

Having sat down behind the *nidhana* of the *sāman*, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the Gandharva-formulas: "O Viśvāvasu, Soma-Gandharva... from the womb, do not diminish. Having climbed up onto the other *mahāvīra* vessel, he offers six oblations to Pūṣan: "To Pūṣan, svāhā! To Pūṣan, the protector of paths, svāhā! To Pūṣan, the winner of men, svāhā! To Pūṣan, the swift-footed, svāhā! To Pūṣan, the purifier, svāhā! To Pūṣan, the one of the *sāketa* settlement, svāhā!"—thus [he offers].
He pays homage with: "Thou art named Ranti; thou art the divine Gandharva... do not harm me."

Having covered [the cauldron] well with a black antelope skin, while descending, he mutters: "O divine Gharma, as a god you have sat upon this; come after me, together with offspring, together with the abundance of wealth. Having descended, he says, "Sprinkle around!

Taking a water-pot, the sprinkler goes around three times, sprinkling by moving to the right. He scoops up [the water] for the sake of cleansing, saying: "You are lovely, the suckling of the nourisher, the child of the progenitor."
Having set down the pitcher, he runs around three times in the opposite direction;
then, having gone toward the north, they purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit with the formula, "O friends, we do not hate him whom we [formerly] hated.
Then they worship the sun with the verse, "Up from the darkness, we have risen... etc.
Then, having gone back toward the west, he offers an oblation to Sūrya at the Gārhapatya fire with the verse, "Upwards that bright one," and thus the Pravargya rite is completed;
the ritual pertaining to the Agniṣṭoma becomes established.
